title: Fact, Opinion, and Inference
subtitle: Learn to identify different types of statements and support them with evidence.
objectives: Identify statements as facts, opinions, or inferences.
Explain the difference between facts, opinions, and inferences.
Provide evidence to support facts and inferences, and recognize that opinions are personal views.

scenes.title: What's the Difference?
scenes.display: Is it true? Or just what someone thinks?
scenes.narration: Do you wonder if statements are true or feelings? We learn facts, opinions, and inferences today. This skill helps you understand information better.
scenes.visualAction: A thought bubble appears with a question mark. Two cartoon characters, one with a 'fact' label and one with an 'opinion' label, look at each other curiously.

scenes.title: Define the Terms
scenes.display: Fact: Proven. Opinion: Feeling. Inference: Guess.
scenes.narration: A fact is provable. An opinion is a personal feeling. An inference is a conclusion from evidence. Think like a detective, finding clues.
scenes.visualAction: Three distinct cards slide onto the screen, each with a definition and a simple icon: a checkmark for fact, a thought bubble for opinion, and a magnifying glass for inference.

scenes.title: See It in Action
scenes.narration: A report states six teams participated; that's a fact. 'The game was exciting' is an opinion. 'It might attract more teams' is an inference.
scenes.visualAction: A document icon appears, then highlights sections as narration explains: 'six teams participated' (fact), 'game was exciting' (opinion), 'might attract more teams' (inference). Simple animations show checking, thinking, and guessing.

scenes.title: Quick Check
scenes.narration: Facts are objective and verifiable. Opinions are subjective and personal. Inferences are reasoned guesses. This helps you evaluate information critically.
scenes.visualAction: The three definition cards from 'explain' reappear. A cartoon character points to each card as its definition is briefly reviewed. A 'thumbs up' icon appears.

scenes.title: Improve Your Statement
scenes.narration: Always ask: Can this be proven? If not, state it as your view. Explain evidence for inferences. This makes your statements clearer.
scenes.visualAction: A cartoon character tries to push a square peg into a round hole (weak statement). Then, the character easily places a round peg into a round hole, with a thought bubble showing 'evidence' (strong statement).

scenes.title: Your Turn to Classify
scenes.narration: Now, classify statements as fact, opinion, or inference. Then, explain your reasoning. Remember to look for all the important clues and evidence!
scenes.visualAction: A stack of cards with question marks appears. A cartoon hand reaches out to pick one. A thought bubble with 'Fact? Opinion? Inference?' appears above the cards.

scenes.title: You're a Statement Sleuth!
scenes.narration: You've learned to distinguish facts, opinions, and inferences well. This skill improves understanding, communication, and decisions. Keep practicing to become a statement sleuth!
scenes.visualAction: A cartoon character wearing a detective hat gives a confident nod. A large 'A+' or 'star' icon appears, then fades out.

reading.title: Understanding Statements
reading.text: Statements come in different forms. A fact is a piece of information that can be proven true or false with evidence. An opinion is a personal belief or judgment that cannot be proven. An inference is a conclusion reached by combining facts with reasoning. Knowing the type helps you evaluate information.

reading.title: Applying the Concepts
reading.text: Consider a fictional art show. 'The show featured 20 paintings' is a fact; you can count them. 'The blue painting was the best' is an opinion; others might prefer a different one. 'The artist likely spent many hours on each piece' is an inference, based on the detail and number of paintings.

reading.title: Why It Matters
reading.text: Distinguishing between facts, opinions, and inferences is crucial for critical thinking. It helps you avoid mistaking personal views for objective truths and allows you to build arguments on solid evidence. This skill is vital for academic success and everyday decision-making.

materials.title: Fictional Art Show Review
materials.text: The annual 'Canvas Dreams' art show, held last Saturday, showcased 20 unique paintings from local artists. The vibrant colors and intricate details of 'Ocean's Embrace,' a large blue abstract, truly captured the audience's attention. Many attendees commented on its beauty. The artist, known for their meticulous work, likely spent many hours on each piece. Overall, it was a truly inspiring exhibition, and I believe it was the best show this gallery has hosted all year.

promptExamples.initial: The blue painting was the best.
promptExamples.improved: In my opinion, the blue painting was the best because its vibrant colors truly captured my attention.
promptExamples.followup: That's a good start! To make it even clearer, you could add that 'many attendees commented on its beauty,' which is a fact from the review that supports your opinion about its impact.

activity.title: Statement Classification Challenge
activity.instructions: Read the 'Fictional Art Show Review' material. For each statement below, classify it as a Fact, Opinion, or Inference. Then, write a brief justification for your choice, explaining why it fits that category.
activity.starter:
1. The 'Canvas Dreams' art show was held last Saturday.
2. 'Ocean's Embrace' was the best painting in the show.
3. The artist likely spent many hours on each piece.
4. The show featured 20 unique paintings.
5. The exhibition was truly inspiring.
activity.expectedEvidence: A list of classifications (Fact, Opinion, or Inference) for each statement, along with a short justification for each classification.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a FACT?
options: The annual 'Canvas Dreams' art show showcased 20 unique paintings.
The blue abstract painting was the most beautiful.
The gallery will host an even better show next year.
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is a fact because the number of paintings (20) can be verified by counting them in the review. Options 1 and 2 are opinions or inferences that cannot be objectively proven.

quiz.question: Which of the following is an OPINION?
options: The artist is known for meticulous work.
The vibrant colors of 'Ocean's Embrace' truly captured the audience's attention.
The 'Canvas Dreams' show was the best this gallery has hosted all year.
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is an opinion because 'best' is a subjective judgment that cannot be proven true or false. Option 0 is a fact stated in the review. Option 1 describes an effect on the audience, which is a verifiable observation.

quiz.question: Based on the 'Fictional Art Show Review', which statement is an INFERENCE?
options: The show featured paintings from local artists.
The artist likely spent many hours on each piece.
Many attendees commented on the beauty of 'Ocean's Embrace'.
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is an inference because it's a conclusion drawn from the fact that the artist is 'known for their meticulous work' and the 'intricate details' of the paintings. Options 0 and 2 are facts directly stated in the review.

mission.title: Create Your Own Review
mission.instructions: Imagine you visited a fictional science fair. Write a short review (3-5 sentences) about one project. Include at least one fact, one opinion, and one inference about the project. Clearly label each type of statement you use.
rubric: Includes at least one clearly labeled fact.
Includes at least one clearly labeled opinion.
Includes at least one clearly labeled inference.
All labels correctly identify the statement type.

hints.question: How do I know if something is a fact?
hints.answer: A fact is something that can be proven true or false with evidence. Look for specific details, numbers, dates, or events that can be verified.

hints.question: What's the difference between an opinion and an inference?
hints.answer: An opinion is a personal feeling or belief. An inference is a conclusion you reach based on facts and logical reasoning, even if it's not directly stated. Opinions are subjective; inferences are reasoned guesses.

hints.question: How can I support my classifications in the activity?
hints.answer: For a fact, explain what makes it verifiable. For an opinion, state that it's a personal feeling or judgment. For an inference, explain which facts from the text led you to that conclusion.

educatorNotes.sampleAnswer:
Activity Sample Answer:
1. The 'Canvas Dreams' art show was held last Saturday. (Fact) - This can be verified by checking the event schedule.
2. 'Ocean's Embrace' was the best painting in the show. (Opinion) - 'Best' is a subjective judgment; others might prefer a different painting.
3. The artist likely spent many hours on each piece. (Inference) - This is concluded from the text mentioning the artist's 'meticulous work' and the 'intricate details' of the paintings.
4. The show featured 20 unique paintings. (Fact) - This is a specific number that can be counted and verified.
5. The exhibition was truly inspiring. (Opinion) - 'Inspiring' is a personal feeling or judgment, not something that can be objectively proven.

Mission Sample Answer:
My visit to the 'Future Innovations' science fair was fascinating! (Opinion) - I found the 'Eco-Friendly Water Filter' project particularly impressive. (Opinion) The project demonstrated how to purify water using natural materials, and the student explained that it filtered 1 liter of water in 10 minutes. (Fact) Based on the clear demonstration and the detailed logbook, the student must have conducted extensive experiments to achieve these results. (Inference)
educatorNotes.commonMisconception: A common misconception is confusing an inference with a fact. Learners might think if something is 'highly likely' or 'obvious' it's a fact, rather than a conclusion based on facts.
reviewChecks: Are justifications clear and directly related to the definition of fact, opinion, or inference?
For inferences, does the justification clearly link to supporting facts from the text?
For opinions, is it clear that the statement is a personal belief and not presented as objective truth?
educatorNotes.safetyNotes: Ensure students understand that while opinions are personal, they should always be expressed respectfully and considerately, especially when discussing others' work or ideas.
